newsitem.title: USA: Port of New York/New Jersey says '96 results mixed.
newsitem.headline: Port of New York/New Jersey says '96 results mixed.

text.p: Container traffic declined in 1996 at the Port of New York and New Jersey, while the harbor's market share held steady in what officials said was a "mixed" year for the East Coast's biggest port.
"Clearly, we had a mixed year for the Harbor in 1996," Lillian Borrone, director of the Commerce Department at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, told reporters on Thursday.

"On the one hand...it was a relatively flat year, not only for our port, but for the entire domestic North Atlantic port market as well," she added. "On the other hand, we arrested a two-year decline in our market share among domestic North Atlantic ports..."

The flow of containerized goods, known as general cargo and made up largely of consumer merchandise, edged lower in 1996. New York also continued to lose business to the fast-growing port of Halifax, Nova Scotia, Borrone said.
But activity in a few sectors, namely bulk cargo, autombiles and intermodal shipments, posted gains on the year.

In addition, Borrone cited a number of developments during 1996 that had "positive ramifications" for the port, including a new labor agreement with port employees, the re-opening of Howland Hook container terminal in Staten Island, and expanding use of on-dock rail.
Container traffic declined by 1.7 percent in 1996, from 14.6 million long tons in 1995 to 14.3 million long tons in 1996. No dollar-value figures were available.
Imports of general cargo fell by 1.4 percent to 9.5 million tons, while exports decreased by 2.0 percent to 4.9 million tons.
By contrast, bulk cargo activity was up substantially in 1996, fueled mainly by sharply higher imports of heating fuel and road salt during 1996's unusally harsh winter.
Motor vehicle imports and exports also posted increases in 1996, rising three percent to a nation-leading 413,000 passenger cars.

The biggest declines were posted in military cargo and paper goods, she said. Military imports into New York sank 37 percent, due largely to the pending closure of the Military Ocean Terminal in Bayonne, New Jersey.

While waste paper continues to be the port's leading export commodity, overall export volumes fell by a hefty 21 percent on the year. Port officials attributed the decline to greater domestic use of recyled paper.
Alcoholic beverages continued to be the top import into the harbor, rising 3.7 percent in 1996 to 733,009 tons.

Meanwhile, New York remained the busiest port in the North Atlantic, handling twice as much volume as the number-two port of Norfolk, Virginia. New York's portion of the U.S. North Atlantic market held steady at 38 percent.

But the Port of Halifax, aided by naturally deep shipping channels and lower harbor taxes, continued to siphon off market share from New York. Officials estimated that New York lost out on some 90,000 containers to Halifax last year.

The diversion of cargo to Halifax has been a top concern in New York for years. While Halifax can accommodate newer and larger container vessels, New York Harbor must be continually dredged to make its channels passable.

What to do with the millions of yards of sludge that build up in the harbor each year has become a sometimes contentious political issue, as officials race to come up with alternative disposal areas before a key offshore dumpsite is shut down in September.

While many shippers and carriers have complained that dredging has been proceeding too slowly, environmentalists have raised objections to testing and disposal methods for the dredged material, much of which is contaminated.

Port officials expect maintenance dredging of the harbor's key channels to be stepped up this spring, and Barrone said she was optimistic a consensus would soon emerge over how to take the harbor to a more competitive depth of 45 feet.

"I think we made some significant progress last year, and I think we're poised to make additional significant progresss this year," Borrone said. "I would hope...that we could see the 45-foot program begin as early as October of this year."
